To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the root-mean-square gain of a switched linear system is equal to the root-mean-square of a switched linear equation with the same state space, and (ii) the root-mean- square gain of a switched first-order system with n states can be characterized by solving n differential Riccati inequalities.

(i) the RMS gain problem can be formulated as a variational problem; (ii) the WCSL can often be found explicitly; (iii) the WCSL has no more than two switchings; (iv) the WCSL is unique for first-order systems; and (v) the WCSL for first-order systems can be found in closed form.

(1) the RMS gain of a first-order switched linear system is equal to the largest of the RMS gains corresponding to the individual subsystems; (2) the RMS gain is equal to the maximal possible gain if and only if the system is first-order; (3) for first-order switched linear systems, the maximal possible gain is equal to a certain convex combination of the gains corresponding to the linear components.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the root-mean-square (RMS)-gain problem for switched systems.

a new approach to the RMS gain analysis of switched linear systems, which can be viewed as an attempt to extend the results obtained by the authors in the context of switched linear systems with constant switching laws to the general switched linear systems with time-varying switching laws.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the WCSL is a piecewise constant function of time with no more than 2 pieces.
the WCSL for first-order systems can always be characterized using two switches, and the RMS gain can be computed by solving two Riccati equations.
the RMS gain problem is completely solved for the first-order case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel approach to the RMS gain of switched linear control systems, based on a variational characterization.
, for the switched linear systems we considered, the RMS gain is a piecewise affine function of the initial condition.
we have provided an alternative approach to the computation of RMS gains of switched systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the WCSL problem is a variational one and can be solved using variational tools.
the RMS gain problem can be reduced to a finite-dimensional optimization problem, which is much simpler to solve than the original infinite-dimensional problem.
the RMS gain can be characterized by solving a finite number of differential Riccati inequalities, even though there is an infinite number of switching strategies.
